items.gist: The rite of abhiṣeka is introduced; the guru transfers authority to a worthy, knowledgeable disciple, and one lacking this knowledge is not a true teacher.
A guru must know the sixfold path; even without other marks, knowledge makes one a guru.
The guru is learned, devoted, and compassionate; self-born status and other disqualifications are discussed, with Śrīpūrva not imposing rigid restrictions.
Qualifications vary by tantra; karmita teachers exclude certain persons, and knowledge outweighs birth or bodily marks.
The guru initiates with mantras and gifts, then teaches essentials; the initiated guru serves disciples through seven sattras.
A knowledgeless guru transfers authority and ceases to initiate; the former guru remains free and is called ācārya when teaching rightly.
The guru must not initiate proudly; after abhiṣeka he practices mantras for six months, awakening subtle nāda and mantra power.
Mantra pervades the cakras; after completing vidyāvrata, mantras become powerful and act for the disciple's authority.
The guru initiates only worthy disciples, testing them; divine will and the disciple's desire indicate true worthiness.
A disciple who lacks trust may have knowledge withdrawn through meditation on the leftward vāmā śakti.
Withdrawal applies only to unrooted knowledge; the Śiva-identical guru, acting in fivefold creation, attains full authority.
